body_markdown:
Calls are only part of a contact center’s workload. Agents also have to find customer information, reply to messages, update cases, and document what happened, often with the next customer already waiting. Growing demand often brings a familiar dilemma for[contact centers](https://sangoma.com/products/contact-center-as-a-service/) : hire more people, ask existing teams to handle more, or find ways to take some of the work off their hands.


AI can answer routine inquiries, retrieve customer information, and prepare call summaries. But not everything that can be automated is worth automating. A system that gives inaccurate answers or can’t access the right customer records may leave agents with even more to sort out. Before investing, contact center leaders need a realistic idea of[what AI can take over](https://sangoma.com/products/sangoma-ai/) , how it will fit with their existing systems, and whether the benefits will justify the investment.


## What Makes an AI Contact Center Different From a Traditional One?


Traditional contact centers rely largely on agents, fixed[interactive voice response](https://sangoma.com/blog/ai-receptionist-vs-ivr-vs-virtual-agent-what-small-businesses-actually-need/) (IVR) menus, and scripted bots. Menus and scripts work well for predictable requests but struggle when customers say something unexpected or stray from the available options. AI-powered systems can interpret a customer’s intent even when the wording changes, allowing people to explain their problems in their own words.


Behind the conversation, speech-to-text converts spoken words into text, and natural language processing identifies what the customer is asking. Machine learning can uncover patterns in customer interactions, while generative AI helps agents draft replies and summarize calls.


Businesses can introduce AI into an existing[cloud contact center](https://sangoma.com/blog/what-is-cloud-contact-center/) without handing every customer conversation over to automation. Routine requests, call summaries, and information searches can be automated or AI-assisted, while agents handle cases that need investigation or human judgement.


AI can play several distinct roles. **Customer-facing AI agents** handle routine requests directly; **agent-assist tools** support employees during conversations; and **AI analytics** helps managers identify patterns and improve operations. A business may use one or several of these capabilities, depending on its needs.


## Common AI Use Cases in the Contact Center


AI can help route an incoming request, support the employee who handles it, and review the conversation afterward. The following applications address different parts of that process.


### 24/7 Self-Service AI Agents for Routine Requests


[AI voice agents and chatbots](https://sangoma.com/blog/chat-ai-vs-voice-ai-which-is-better-for-your-business/) can answer common questions and handle routine requests outside staffed hours, from checking order statuses to booking appointments.


How far AI can go depends on its integrations and permissions. A chatbot drawing on help articles might explain how to reschedule an appointment. An AI agent connected to a scheduling system could find another slot, confirm the change with the customer, and update the booking. Agentic AI goes beyond generating answers by coordinating multiple steps and taking permitted actions through connected systems, within the approval rules and safeguards set by the business.


### Conversational IVR and Intelligent Call Routing


Conversational IVR lets callers explain what they need in their own words, without navigating numbered menus. AI interprets the request and routes the call using information such as customer records, language preferences, and agent skills.


### Real-Time Agent Assist


Agent-assist tools work alongside employees during customer conversations, pulling up relevant knowledge articles, retrieving account details, or suggesting responses.


For written conversations,[Sangoma CX AI Assist](https://sangoma.com/products/sangoma-ai/) helps agents draft and edit replies across SMS, WhatsApp, and email. Agents can shorten a message, correct grammar, or adjust its tone before reviewing and sending it.


### Call Transcription and Automated Summaries


[AI call transcription](https://sangoma.com/blog/how-ai-call-transcription-improve-customer-service/) creates a searchable record of conversations, while automated summaries capture what the customer needed, what was agreed, and any outstanding follow-ups. Automated summaries can reduce the time agents spend writing notes and can pick up previous cases without replaying entire calls. Important details, particularly names, amounts, and commitments, still need checking.


[Sangoma Scribe](https://sangoma.com/products/scribe/) offers call and voicemail transcription, summaries, and sentiment analysis on supported Sangoma communications platforms.


### Quality Assurance and Sentiment Analysis


Supervisors rarely have time to listen to every call. Depending on the platform, AI-powered quality assurance can evaluate a larger share of eligible recorded or transcribed interactions, flagging missed verification steps, possible policy violations, and signs of customer frustration for human review. Coverage depends on the supported channels, languages, recording availability, and licensing.


Sentiment analysis can also help identify interactions worth investigating, although sarcasm, context, and transcription errors can skew the results. Automated scores are useful for prioritizing reviews, but shouldn’t determine an agent’s performance rating without human assessment.


### Analytics, Forecasting, and Workforce Planning


AI can identify recurring customer issues that might otherwise go unnoticed. A sudden increase in questions about delivery options, for instance, could reveal confusing checkout instructions or a fulfillment problem.


Forecasting tools use historical contact volumes to predict demand and help managers plan staffing around expected workloads, handling times, and agent availability. Promotions, outages, and other unexpected events still need to be factored into those plans.


For more on what to measure, see Sangoma’s[contact center analytics guide](https://sangoma.com/blog/contact-center-analytics/) .


## Examples of Contact Center AI in Action


The following are illustrative examples of what AI could support, not functions included with every AI contact center product. Each requires supported integrations, appropriate identity checks, defined permissions, applicable privacy and regulatory safeguards, and human escalation for situations that need judgment or authorized decisions.


### Healthcare


Prescription refill updates: Patients can check whether a prescription is ready or still awaiting approval without necessarily waiting to speak to pharmacy staff. With access to the pharmacy system, AI can provide an up-to-date status, while clinical questions stay with qualified professionals.


Specialist coverage and authorization: Patients can check the status of a prior authorization and find out whether any paperwork is outstanding. AI can explain the documented next steps, although questions about coverage decisions and payment guarantees still need human attention.


### Retail and Hospitality


Returns and refunds: For straightforward returns, AI can check the purchase against the return policy, initiate the return, and generate a shipping label. Staff can concentrate on disputed refunds and exceptions that need a decision.


Requests during a hotel stay: A guest reporting broken air conditioning doesn’t necessarily need the front desk to relay the problem to maintenance. AI connected to the hotel’s systems can log the request against the correct room and notify the maintenance team. Staff still handle repairs and room changes.


### Financial Services


Suspicious transactions: A suspected fraudulent charge needs specialist attention, but the initial information gathering can be automated. After customer authentication, AI can collect transaction details and open a dispute case, giving the fraud team a useful starting point for its investigation.


Loan application follow-ups: Sometimes an application is delayed because a document is missing. AI connected to the lending system can identify what’s outstanding and explain how to submit it, without involving a loan officer in a routine status inquiry.


## Advantages of AI-Powered Contact Center Solutions


The benefits of contact center AI depend on whether it helps customers complete their requests and reduces the work required to serve them. Response speed, resolution quality, and operating costs all deserve attention.


### Benefits for Your Customers


Customers can get help with routine requests after hours and avoid waiting for an agent during busy periods. Using a maintained source of information can also reduce conflicting answers from different channels.


When a conversation moves to an employee, passing along the history saves the customer from explaining the problem again. Fewer delays and repeated explanations make service easier to use.


### Benefits for Your Agents


Less time spent searching for answers and documenting calls leaves agents more time to investigate difficult cases. Suggested replies also reduce the effort involved in writing routine messages.


As AI takes on simpler requests, the remaining queue may contain more complex or emotionally demanding conversations. Managers should adjust workload expectations and coaching to reflect the work agents are actually handling.


### Benefits for Your Business


Handling more inquiries with the same team can reduce overtime or postpone additional hiring. Consistent service processes can help maintain quality as volumes change.


Conversation analysis also gives managers evidence of problems elsewhere in the business. Fixing a confusing policy or a recurring order issue may prevent future calls altogether.


Measure the cost per resolved issue alongside repeat contacts and customer satisfaction. A cheaper interaction offers little value if the customer has to call again.


## Keeping the Humans in the Loop


AI can handle a routine request in seconds, but what happens when it gets something wrong, can’t find the information it needs, or encounters a situation that calls for human judgment? Contact centers need clear rules for when agents should step in, what information they receive, and how problems with the AI are identified and corrected.


### Let Human Agents Handle Complex and Sensitive Interactions


A bereavement-related account request, a disputed charge, or an unusual complaint may need a person who can consider the circumstances and make an appropriate decision.


Set escalation rules for sensitive requests, repeated misunderstandings, missing information, and actions outside the system’s authority. Customers should also be able to ask for a person directly.


### Preserve Context During AI-to-Human Handoffs


The receiving agent needs to know what the customer wants, which records are relevant, what has already been attempted, and why the conversation was transferred.


Make the summary and conversation history available in the agent’s workspace. Clearly distinguish completed actions from failed attempts. If a refund was never submitted, the agent should not have to discover the failure by questioning the customer. Only the information the receiving agent needs should be shared, with sensitive details protected by appropriate access controls.


For after-hours requests, explain the next step accurately, whether that means creating a callback request or directing the customer to an available support team.


### Improve AI Performance Through Human Oversight and Feedback


Give agents a simple way to report incorrect answers, poor suggestions, and failed transfers. Supervisors should also review a sample of conversations marked successful, since a customer leaving the conversation does not prove that the issue was resolved.


Assign someone to investigate recurring errors, update the relevant content, and adjust the workflow. Test the affected requests again before releasing a change.


## Common Challenges of Contact Center AI Adoption


Customer records are incomplete, policies change, and phone systems don’t always play nicely with other software. AI has to work with the contact center you’ve actually got, including its less-than-perfect parts.


### Fragmented Data and Outdated Knowledge Content


If your CRM says one thing and your help center says another, which answer will AI give the customer? Decide which source the AI should trust for each type of information and who is responsible for keeping it current. Pay particular attention to prices, return policies, and eligibility rules, where outdated information can quickly become an expensive problem.


### Integrating AI With Existing Contact Center Systems


Connecting AI to your phone system doesn’t automatically give it access to customer records or the ability to update them. Older PBXs, customized CRMs, and separate applications across locations may require additional development.


If you’re using a[hosted PBX](https://sangoma.com/blog/hosted-pbx-features-benefits-and-the-best-providers/) , check which integrations are supported and what needs custom work. Have vendors demonstrate a complete request, including retrieving information, updating a record, and transferring the conversation to an agent. Then ask them to show what happens when the CRM is unavailable or an update fails.


### Data Privacy, Security, and Compliance Risks


Adding an AI service may also mean sharing customer data with another provider.


Before deployment, establish where the data goes, who can access it, how long it’s retained, and whether it’s used to train AI models. Check recording consent requirements and applicable industry regulations. AI integrations should have access only to the information and actions they need.


### Inaccurate Responses and AI Hallucinations


An AI assistant can sound confident while presenting an incorrect account balance or inventing a policy.


For answers involving customer accounts, bookings, and prices, require information from current, approved sources. Test the system with incomplete records, ambiguous questions, and requests it shouldn’t be able to answer. If it can’t verify the information, it needs to admit that and involve an employee.


### Over-Automation and Poor Customer Experiences


Nobody wants to spend five minutes arguing with a chatbot just to reach a person. Make it easy for customers to request an agent, especially after repeated misunderstandings.


And don’t judge automation solely by how many conversations it handles without human involvement. Look at abandoned interactions, failed transfers, and customers who call back because their original problem wasn’t resolved.


### Agent Resistance and Change Management


Agents will notice things that don’t show up in vendor demonstrations: suggested replies that need extensive rewriting, incorrect call summaries, or AI quality scores that misinterpret a difficult conversation.


Bring employees into the pilot, train them to review and correct AI output, and give them a straightforward way to report problems. Be clear about how automated performance evaluations will be used and how agents can challenge inaccurate assessments. Their feedback should influence which workflows get automated and how the system is improved.


## The Cost of Implementing AI in a Contact Center


Compare proposals using the same expected usage and contract period. A low monthly subscription may come with separate charges for implementation, AI usage, or support.


### Common AI Call Center Pricing Models


Vendors may combine several billing models within one proposal.


Pricing model What you pay for What to check


Per seat Licensed users Named or concurrent seats, minimum commitments, and AI add-ons


Per minute Audio time handled or processed Included minutes, rounding, telephony charges, and overage rates


Per resolution or outcome Conversations meeting the vendor’s billing definition How abandonment, transfers, and reopened cases are counted


Platform fee Access to a service or feature package Included channels, usage allowances, support, and optional features


### What Drives the Cost Up or Down?


Higher contact volumes and longer calls can increase usage charges. Additional channels, languages, or AI features may require a different plan. Custom integrations generally involve more work than a connection the vendor already supports.


Separate upfront expenses from ongoing costs. Initial work may include configuration, knowledge-base cleanup, integration development, testing, and staff training.


Recurring expenses can include subscriptions, AI processing, maintenance, premium support, and staff time spent reviewing results. Confirm whether third-party AI services are included and request estimates for both typical usage and busy periods.


### How to Estimate the ROI of AI-Powered Contact Center Software


Calculate benefits and costs over the same period:


ROI (%) = \[(Financial benefits − Total investment) ÷ Total investment\] × 100


Start with current contact volumes, handling time, after-call work, and cost per interaction. Use pilot results to estimate how much time AI saves after accounting for review and corrections. The following hypothetical example calculates the potential value of time saved, not guaranteed cash savings. It assumes the full eligible call volume benefits from summaries throughout the year and that the estimated one-minute saving is net of agents checking and correcting the output.


For example, suppose a team handles 10,000 eligible calls a month. Automated summaries save one minute per call after agents check the notes. At a total labor cost of $30 per hour, the saved time is worth:


10,000 calls × 1 minute ÷ 60 × $30 = $5,000 per month


Over a full year, the estimated value is $60,000.


Assume the first-year costs are:


Cost Illustrative amount


Software and usage $24,000


Implementation and integration $10,000


Training $2,000


Ongoing maintenance $4,000


**Total investment** **$40,000**


The calculation becomes:


Illustrative ROI based on the value of time saved: \[($60,000 − $40,000) ÷ $40,000\] × 100 = **50%**


This example assigns a financial value to capacity freed up for other work; it does not necessarily represent a reduction in spending. Actual cash savings occur when the business can reduce costs, such as overtime, outsourced handling, or additional hiring. Calculate realized savings separately from productivity gains.


Adjust the estimate for rollout time and adoption. Avoid counting the same saved minutes twice under shorter handling time and reduced documentation, and compare the results with pre-implementation service metrics. For a real-world estimate, adjust for adoption rates, ineligible interactions, recording or transcription failures, and the ramp-up period.


## How to Choose Your AI Contact Center Software


Don’t let vendors choose the demo scenarios. Bring a few real customer requests from your contact center and see how the software handles them. Compare products based on the tasks you actually need to automate, how well they fit your existing environment, and whether they improve customer outcomes.


### Step 1: Identify Which Customer Requests to Automate


Start with frequent, repetitive requests that consume agent time and can be handled reliably by AI. Good early candidates may include basic FAQs, status checks, and straightforward routing. Keep complex complaints, sensitive situations, and consequential decisions with a person, or establish clear approval and escalation steps.


**Ask vendors:** Which requests can the system resolve without additional integrations? How does it recognize that a request needs human assistance?


### Step 2: Check Integrations and Compatibility


Confirm what the AI can read from and write to your existing contact center, phone system, CRM, scheduling tools, and knowledge sources. An integration that simply displays a customer record is different from one that can complete a transaction. If you use an existing[hosted PBX](https://sangoma.com/blog/hosted-pbx-features-benefits-and-the-best-providers/) , verify the voice and data connections separately.


**Ask vendors:** Which integrations are built in, which require custom development, and what happens if a system is unavailable during a conversation?


### Step 3: Evaluate AI Capabilities Using Real Scenarios


Use representative interactions from your operation, including different accents, interruptions, vague questions, incomplete records, and customers asking for an agent. Verify whether the AI can answer accurately, complete permitted actions, and hand off without losing context. Compare supported channels, languages, reporting, and privacy controls rather than relying on a general AI feature label.


**Ask vendors:** Can you demonstrate a completed task using our actual workflow? Can supervisors review outcomes and tell whether the customer’s issue was resolved rather than merely contained?


### Step 4: Run a Pilot Before Committing


Test a limited set of interactions before a full rollout. Agree on success criteria in advance: successful resolutions, repeat contacts, transfer failures, response times, agent time saved after corrections, customer satisfaction, and total costs. Include failure scenarios: unavailable integrations, misunderstood requests, unanswered questions, and an unavailable transfer destination. Keep a way to return to your existing process if the pilot fails.


**Ask vendors:** What reporting is available during the pilot? How do we escalate problems, change a workflow, or switch back without disrupting customers?


## Frequently Asked Questions About AI Contact Centers


### What is the difference between AI agents and AI agent-assist tools?


AI agents interact directly with customers to answer questions or complete supported workflows. Agent-assist tools help employees by suggesting replies, finding information, or preparing summaries. AI analytics examines interaction data to identify trends and service improvements.


### How much does AI contact center software cost?


There is no single standard price. Vendors may charge per seat, per minute, per completed resolution, through a platform fee, or through a combination of models. Compare the full cost of software, telephony, AI processing, integration, setup, training, support, and any overages under the same usage assumptions.


### Can AI contact center software work with an existing phone system?


Often, but compatibility depends on the platform and use case. Basic AI assistance may be easier to introduce than live voice automation or tasks requiring CRM updates. Ask vendors to demonstrate the connection to your actual phone and business systems before committing.


### How do you measure whether contact center AI is successful?


Measure successful task completion, first contact resolution, repeat contacts, customer satisfaction, escalations, and the net time agents save after reviewing AI output. Compare results against your pre-implementation baseline. Containment alone does not prove that a customer received the help they needed.
